routes.label: Extend a segment to create similar triangles

question:
Triangle \(ABC\) and point \(P\) in the same plane are given. Point \(P\) is equidistant from \(A\) and \(B,\) angle \(APB\) is twice angle \(ACB,\) and \(\overline{AC}\) intersects \(\overline{BP}\) at point \(D.\) If \(PB=3\) and \(PD=2,\) then \(AD\cdot CD=\)

[Figure 1](figures/1997_AMC_12_Q26_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The doubled angle suggests constructing an isosceles triangle whose base angles equal \(\angle ACB\). Let \(\theta=\angle ACB\). Since \(PA=PB=3\), extend \(BP\) beyond \(P\) to a point \(Q\) with \(PQ=3\). Then \(PA=PQ\).

Because \(D\) lies on segment \(BP\), the points occur in the order \(B,D,P,Q\), giving
\[
DB=3-2=1,\qquad DQ=2+3=5.
\]
We also need \(D\) strictly inside \(AC\). It cannot equal \(A\), since \(PA=3\ne PD\). If \(D=C\), then \(\angle ACB\) would be an exterior angle of triangle \(APC\), greater than \(\angle APC=\angle APB=2\theta\), contradicting \(\angle ACB=\theta\). Thus \(A,D,C\) occur in that order.

The rays \(PB\) and \(PQ\) are opposite, so \(\angle APQ=180^\circ-2\theta\). The equal base angles of isosceles triangle \(APQ\) are therefore
\[
\angle AQP=\angle PAQ
=\frac{180^\circ-(180^\circ-2\theta)}2
=\theta.
\]
Consequently, \(\angle AQD=\angle BCD=\theta\). At \(D\), the intersecting lines give equal vertical angles \(\angle ADQ=\angle BDC\). Hence \(\triangle DAQ\sim\triangle DBC\) by two equal angles.

Corresponding sides connect the desired product to the known lengths:
\[
\frac{AD}{DB}=\frac{DQ}{DC}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
AD\cdot CD=DB\cdot DQ=1\cdot5=5.
\]
The denominators are positive because \(DB=1\) and \(D\ne C\). Thus the answer is \(\boxed{5}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).

solutionMethods.explanation:
The product \(AD\cdot CD\) suggests making \(AC\) a chord of a circle through \(A\) and \(B\). Construct the circle with center \(P\) and radius \(3\). Since \(PA=PB=3\), both \(A\) and \(B\) lie on it. Extend \(BP\) beyond \(P\) to \(Q\), where \(PQ=3\); then \(BQ\) is a diameter.

The segment conditions give the order \(B,D,P,Q\), so
\[
DB=3-2=1,\qquad DQ=2+3=5.
\]
Also, \(D\ne A\), because \(PA\ne PD\). To exclude \(D=C\), write \(\theta=\angle ACB\). If \(D=C\), the exterior-angle property in triangle \(APC\) would give \(\theta>\angle APC=2\theta\), which is impossible. Thus \(D\) is strictly between \(A\) and \(C\).

Because \(PA=PQ\) and \(\angle APQ=180^\circ-2\theta\), the base angles of triangle \(APQ\) equal \(\theta\). In particular,
\[
\angle AQB=\angle AQP=\theta=\angle ACB.
\]
The points \(C\) and \(Q\) are on the same side of line \(AB\). Indeed, \(D\) and \(P\) are on the same side because \(D\) is inside \(BP\); \(C\) lies along ray \(AD\) beyond \(D\), and \(Q\) lies along ray \(BP\) beyond \(P\).

Use the equal-angle cyclicity criterion: two distinct points on the same side of \(AB\) that see \(AB\) under equal angles lie on the same circle through \(A\) and \(B\). It follows that \(A,B,C,Q\) are concyclic, so \(C\) lies on the constructed circle.

Chords \(AC\) and \(BQ\) intersect inside the circle at \(D\). The intersecting-chord theorem equates their segment products:
\[
AD\cdot CD=DB\cdot DQ=1\cdot5=\boxed{5}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
solutionMethods.label: Recognize an intersecting-chord product
